title: Indian Hills Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Indian Hills wells have a 315-foot median depth, 6 gpm median yield, and fractured-bedrock drilling costs to plan for.
h1: Indian Hills Colorado Well and Drilling Guide
intro_html:
Indian Hills sits in mountain ground where most permitted wells draw from unnamed fractured bedrock. Records within 5 miles show a median well depth of 315 feet, but the middle half runs from 163 to 505 feet. That spread matters when you compare rural lots or review a drilling bid.

Water production is also variable. The median reported pump yield is 6.0 gallons per minute, with most reported wells between 3.0 and 9.0 gallons per minute. This page uses Colorado DWR permit records around Indian Hills, including nearby Morrison, Idledale, Kittredge, Genesee, Evergreen, and Dakota Ridge.

sections.heading: Indian Hills well depth follows the mountain bedrock
sections.html:
Indian Hills wells are commonly drilled into fractured granite, gneiss, or other unnamed fractured-bedrock formations. The median reported depth is 315 feet. The middle half of wells falls between 163 and 505 feet, while 20% are 600 feet or deeper. The deepest recorded well reaches 4,095 feet.

For a buyer, that range is more useful than the median alone. A driller bidding a lot near the middle of the local record may be planning a hole around 315 feet, but access, ridge position, fractures, and the specific parcel can move the finished depth substantially. Only 13% of wells are under 100 feet, so a shallow-well assumption is not a sound construction budget.

sections.heading: Plan around a typical 6 gpm well, not a guarantee
sections.html:
The median reported pump yield near Indian Hills is 6.0 gallons per minute. The middle half produces 3.0 to 9.0 gallons per minute. The largest group, 57%, reports between 5 and 15 gallons per minute; 34% report between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, and 3% report under 1 gallon per minute.

That distribution supports many household uses, but it does not promise a particular parcel will perform the same way. Fractured-bedrock wells can make water through limited fractures, so nearby results are useful evidence rather than a guarantee. Ask for the well construction report, pump test information, storage capacity, and any restrictions attached to the permit. A 1 gpm result deserves a different conversation than a 6.0 gpm result, especially for a larger home or irrigation plans.

sections.heading: Water levels changed across the Indian Hills record
sections.html:
Among the wells reporting static water levels, the median depth to water is 100 feet below the surface, with the middle half between 40 and 176 feet. That is the water level when the well is not being pumped, not the same thing as the depth of the well or the water available during pumping.

The decade series does not show a simple continuing decline. Median depth to water was 40 feet in the 1960s and 1970s, 80 feet in the 1980s, and 150 feet in the 1990s. It was 140 feet in the 2010s and 115 feet in the 2020s. The record suggests deeper water levels than the earliest measurements, followed by some recovery, but reporting is limited to 231 wells and should not replace a parcel-specific evaluation.

sections.heading: Indian Hills permit history shows long-running drilling
sections.html:
Permit activity around Indian Hills spans decades. The records contain 113 permits from the 1950s, 279 from the 1960s, 1,372 from the 1970s, 853 from the 1980s, 1,152 from the 1990s, 601 from the 2000s, 375 from the 2010s, and 181 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most frequently named drillers in these records are James Drilling Company, associated with Keaton, Michael K., with 487 wells; Aspen Drilling Company Inc, associated with Beery, Leroy J., with 430; and Living Water Systems Inc., associated with Goble, Robert, with 382. These names help locate comparable permit records. They do not establish current availability, pricing, warranty terms, or performance for a new project.

sections.heading: Indian Hills drilling cost depends heavily on depth
sections.html:
Local ground conditions are fractured mountain bedrock, described in the cost model as granite and gneiss. The typical drilling rate is $65 to $100 per foot. At the local median depth of 315 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $20,500 to $31,500.

A usable water system costs more than the drilled hole. Including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, the modeled finished-well range at that depth is about $26,500 to $43,500. Treat this as a planning range, not a firm quote. A lot that requires a deeper hole, difficult access, more trenching, or additional site work can exceed it. Get the bid in writing and confirm what casing, grout, testing, pump equipment, electrical service, and restoration are included.

sections.heading: Check environmental and site risks before closing
sections.html:
Within about 10 miles of Indian Hills, the mapping shows 81 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 113 historic mine features, and 55 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped sites do not prove that a particular well is contaminated, but they are a reason to review location, groundwater direction, prior land uses, and available test results before buying.

Low yield and dry holes are separate risks in fractured rock. Review neighboring well depths and yields, then have a qualified professional evaluate the proposed location. Septic design, setbacks, driveway access, trench routes, and building placement can affect the project as much as drilling. Confirm the DWR permit allows the intended household use. Exempt household-use wells generally have a 35 gpm pumping limit, and an augmentation plan may be needed in an over-appropriated basin.

sections.heading: Use nearby well records before buying an Indian Hills lot
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, then compare permitted wells near Morrison, Idledale, Kittredge, Genesee, Evergreen, and Dakota Ridge only when their geology and elevation are reasonably similar. Look for reported depth, yield, static water level, construction details, and the age of each record. The local median gives a budget anchor, while the 163-to-505-foot middle range shows why one nearby success is not enough.

For a new build, confirm the water-rights and permit requirements before finalizing plans. Have a driller inspect access and propose a realistic depth range, and have the septic designer consider soil, slope, setbacks, and the well location together. If a property already has a well, test the water and verify the permit and construction record rather than relying on a seller’s description.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Indian Hills, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Indian Hills is 315 feet. The middle half runs from 163 to 505 feet, and 20% of wells are 600 feet or deeper. Mountain fractures, elevation, access, and the individual parcel control the final depth, so the local median is a budget guide rather than a promise.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Indian Hills?
faq.a: The modeled drilling rate for Indian Hills fractured granite and gneiss is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 315-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $20,500 to $31,500. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is modeled at about $26,500 to $43,500.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Indian Hills?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 6.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 3.0 and 9.0 gallons per minute. Most reported wells fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, but 3% report under 1 gallon per minute. Fractured-bedrock production varies by parcel, so request local well reports and testing.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Indian Hills, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from a permit record alone. Within about 10 miles, mapping shows 81 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 113 historic mine features, and 55 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those locations do not prove contamination at your property. Test an existing well, review nearby land uses, and use a qualified laboratory.

faq.q: Are Indian Hills wells in granite or the Denver Basin?
faq.a: Most permitted wells near Indian Hills are identified with unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, including 5,898 wells. The records include 29 alluvial wells and 29 fractured-granite wells. No Denver Basin aquifer wells are recorded in this area. That fractured mountain setting makes depth and yield less predictable than a uniform shallow aquifer.
